physics-paper-1_L5.title: Domestic Electricity, Power and the National Grid
physics-paper-1_L5.content_html:
Domestic Electricity

The UK mains supply is alternating current (a.c.) at about 230 V and a frequency of 50 Hz. This means the current changes direction 50 times per second. Batteries supply direct current (d.c.), which always flows in the same direction.

Key Fact

UK mains supply: alternating current (a.c.), approximately 230 V, frequency 50 Hz. Batteries supply direct current (d.c.).

The Three-Pin Plug

Most appliances connect to the mains via a three-pin plug. The three wires are:

Live wire (brown) — carries the alternating potential difference from the supply. It alternates between about +325 V and −325 V.

Neutral wire (blue) — completes the circuit. It is at, or close to, 0 V (earth potential).

Earth wire (green and yellow) — a safety wire connected to the metal casing of an appliance. It carries current to earth if a fault occurs, preventing electric shock.

The live wire is dangerous even when the switch is off, because it is still at 230 V relative to earth. If you touch it, a large potential difference exists between you and the ground, causing a current to flow through your body. This can cause serious injury or death. A switch is always connected in the live wire so that when it is off, no current can reach the appliance.

Key Fact

The fuse is connected in the live wire. If too much current flows (due to a fault), the fuse wire melts, breaking the circuit and preventing overheating or fire. A circuit breaker does the same job but can be reset instead of replaced.

Electrical Power and Energy Transfer

The power of an appliance tells you how much energy it transfers per second. Two equations link power to current and voltage:

$$P = IV$$

$$P = I^2 R$$

Where \(P\) is power in watts, \(I\) is current in amps, \(V\) is potential difference in volts, and \(R\) is resistance in ohms.

The energy transferred by an appliance depends on its power and how long it is used:

$$E = Pt$$

Where \(E\) is energy in joules, \(P\) is power in watts, and \(t\) is time in seconds. You can also use \(E = QV\), where \(Q\) is charge in coulombs.

A 2 kW kettle is used for 3 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred in joules and in kilowatt-hours.

In joules: \(E = Pt = 2000 \times 180 = 360{,}000\) J

In kWh: \(E = 2 \times \frac{3}{60} = 0.1\) kWh. If electricity costs 30p per kWh, the cost is \(0.1 \times 30 = 3\)p.

The National Grid

The National Grid is a network of cables and transformers that distributes electricity from power stations to homes and businesses across the UK.

Electricity is transmitted at very high voltages (up to 400,000 V) and low currents. Since power lost as heat in the cables equals \(P = I^2 R\), reducing the current dramatically reduces the energy wasted.

Transformers change the voltage of an a.c. supply. A step-up transformer increases the voltage at the power station before transmission. A step-down transformer decreases the voltage near homes to a safe 230 V.

When voltage is increased, current decreases (assuming power stays the same: \(P = IV\)). This is why high-voltage transmission wastes less energy — the lower current means less heating in the cables.

physics-paper-1_L8.title: Atomic Structure, Radioactivity and Half-Life
physics-paper-1_L8.content_html:
The Model of the Atom

Our understanding of atomic structure has developed over time. The first model was the solid sphere model proposed by Dalton in the early 1800s. He imagined atoms as tiny, indivisible balls.

In 1897, J.J. Thomson discovered the electron and proposed the plum pudding model — a sphere of positive charge with negative electrons scattered throughout, like plums in a pudding.

Key Fact

In 1909, Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden fired alpha particles at a thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, but some were deflected and a few bounced back. This proved the atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus with electrons orbiting at a distance — the nuclear model.

Bohr refined the nuclear model by proposing that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances in fixed energy levels (shells). Niels Bohr’s model explained why atoms emit and absorb specific frequencies of electromagnetic radiation.

Later, James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932, completing our picture of the atom: a nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in energy levels.

Radioactive Decay

Some atomic nuclei are radioactive — they are unstable and emit radiation to become more stable. This process is called radioactive decay and is random. You cannot predict when a particular nucleus will decay.

Key Fact

There are three types of nuclear radiation: alpha (\(\alpha\)) particles, beta (\(\beta\)) particles, and gamma (\(\gamma\)) rays. Each has different properties, penetrating power, and ionising ability.

Alpha (\(\alpha\)) — two protons and two neutrons (a helium nucleus). Strongly ionising, stopped by paper or a few centimetres of air. The atomic number decreases by 2 and the mass number decreases by 4.

Beta (\(\beta\)) — a high-speed electron emitted when a neutron turns into a proton. Moderately ionising, stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium. The atomic number increases by 1, mass number stays the same.

Gamma (\(\gamma\)) — an electromagnetic wave with no mass or charge. Weakly ionising, only reduced significantly by several centimetres of lead or thick concrete. The atomic number and mass number are unchanged.

Half-Life

The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time it takes for half the unstable nuclei to decay, or for the count rate (activity) to fall to half its original value.

After one half-life, half the original nuclei remain. After two half-lives, a quarter remain. After three half-lives, one-eighth remain, and so on.

A sample has an activity of 800 Bq. After 30 minutes, the activity is 100 Bq. Calculate the half-life.

800 → 400 → 200 → 100 = three half-lives

Three half-lives = 30 minutes, so one half-life = \(\frac{30}{3} = 10\) minutes.

Uses and Hazards of Radiation

Nuclear radiation has useful applications: gamma rays are used in medical tracers and to sterilise equipment; beta radiation is used in thickness gauges; alpha sources are used in smoke detectors.

Contamination occurs when radioactive material gets onto or inside the body. This is more dangerous because the source stays close to cells. Irradiation is exposure to radiation from an outside source — once the source is removed, the exposure stops.

Precautions include: keeping radioactive sources in lead-lined containers, using tongs to handle sources, wearing protective clothing, and minimising exposure time.

physics-paper-2_L1.title: Forces, Gravity and Resultant Forces
physics-paper-2_L1.content_html:
What Are Forces?

A force is a push or a pull that acts on an object. Forces are measured in newtons (N) and are vector quantities — they have both a magnitude (size) and a direction.

Forces can be contact forces or non-contact forces. Contact forces include friction, air resistance, tension, and normal contact force. Non-contact forces include gravitational, electrostatic, and magnetic forces.

Key Fact

A force is an interaction between two objects. When two objects interact, each exerts a force on the other — these are equal in size and opposite in direction (Newton’s third law).

Gravity and Weight

Gravity is a non-contact force that attracts any two objects with mass. The strength of gravity depends on the masses of the objects and the distance between them.

Weight is the force of gravity acting on an object. It depends on the mass and the gravitational field strength:

$$W = mg$$

Where \(W\) is weight in newtons, \(m\) is mass in kilograms, and \(g\) is gravitational field strength in N/kg. On Earth, \(g \approx 10\) N/kg. On the Moon, \(g \approx 1.6\) N/kg.

Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms. It is the same everywhere. Weight is a force and depends on the gravitational field strength at that location. An astronaut with a mass of 80 kg weighs 800 N on Earth (\(80 \times 10\)) but only 128 N on the Moon (\(80 \times 1.6\)).

Weight is measured using a Newton meter (spring balance). Mass is measured using a balance.

Resultant Forces

When multiple forces act on an object, they can be replaced by a single force that has the same effect. This is called the resultant force.

Key Fact

If forces act in the same direction, add them. If forces act in opposite directions, subtract the smaller from the larger. The resultant force acts in the direction of the larger force.

If the resultant force on an object is zero, the object is in equilibrium. This means it is either stationary or moving at a constant velocity. If the resultant force is not zero, the object will accelerate in the direction of the resultant force.

A free body diagram shows all the forces acting on a single object. Each force is drawn as an arrow starting from the object, with the length of the arrow representing the force’s magnitude and the direction showing which way it acts.

For example, a book on a table has two forces: weight acting downwards and the normal contact force acting upwards. If these are equal, the resultant force is zero and the book stays still.

When two forces do not act along the same line, you can find the resultant using a scale drawing. Draw the forces as arrows, tip-to-tail, to scale. The resultant is the arrow from the start of the first force to the end of the second. Measure its length and angle.

physics-paper-2_L3.title: Speed, Velocity and Acceleration
physics-paper-2_L3.content_html:
Speed and Distance

Speed is a scalar quantity — it tells you how fast something is moving but not the direction. The equation for speed is:

$$s = v t$$

Where \(s\) is distance in metres, \(v\) is speed in m/s, and \(t\) is time in seconds. This can be rearranged to \(v = \frac{s}{t}\).

Key Fact

Typical speeds: walking ~1.5 m/s, running ~3 m/s, cycling ~6 m/s, car in town ~13 m/s, car on motorway ~30 m/s, train ~55 m/s, aeroplane ~250 m/s, sound in air ~330 m/s.

Velocity

Velocity is a vector quantity. It has both magnitude (speed) and direction. An object moving in a circle at constant speed has a changing velocity because its direction is always changing.

The difference between speed and velocity matters in physics: two cars travelling at 30 m/s in opposite directions have the same speed but different velocities.

Acceleration

Acceleration is how quickly an object’s velocity changes. The equation is:

$$a = \frac{\Delta v}{t} = \frac{v - u}{t}$$

Where \(a\) is acceleration in m/s\(^2\), \(v\) is final velocity, \(u\) is initial velocity, and \(t\) is time in seconds. A negative acceleration means the object is decelerating (slowing down).

Key Fact

For uniform (constant) acceleration, use the equation: \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\), where \(s\) is the distance travelled. This is particularly useful when time is not given in the question.

A car accelerates from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 seconds. Calculate the acceleration.

\(a = \frac{v - u}{t} = \frac{30 - 10}{5} = \frac{20}{5} = 4\) m/s\(^2\)

Distance-Time Graphs

A distance-time graph shows how far an object has travelled over time. The gradient (slope) of the line gives the speed.

A horizontal line means the object is stationary. A straight diagonal line means constant speed. A curve getting steeper means the object is accelerating. The steeper the line, the faster the object is moving.

To find the speed at a specific moment on a curved distance-time graph, draw a tangent to the curve at that point. Then calculate the gradient of the tangent: \(\text{speed} = \frac{\text{change in distance}}{\text{change in time}}\).

Velocity-Time Graphs

A velocity-time graph shows how velocity changes over time. The gradient gives the acceleration. The area under the line gives the total distance travelled.

A horizontal line means constant velocity (no acceleration). A line sloping upwards means acceleration. A line sloping downwards means deceleration. The area under the graph can be found by splitting it into rectangles and triangles.

Use a dynamics trolley on a ramp with a light gate or ticker tape timer. Vary the force (by changing the mass on a pulley) while keeping the total mass constant. Measure the acceleration for each force. Plot a graph of force against acceleration — a straight line through the origin shows that \(F = ma\).

physics-paper-2_L4.title: Newton's Laws of Motion
physics-paper-2_L4.content_html:
Newton’s First Law

Newton’s first law states that an object will remain at rest or continue to move at a constant velocity unless a resultant force acts on it.

This means that if all forces on an object are balanced (resultant force = 0), the object will not change its motion. A stationary object stays still. A moving object keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction.

Key Fact

Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist a change in motion. The more mass an object has, the greater its inertia. This is why a heavy object is harder to push into motion or bring to a stop than a light one.

Newton’s Second Law

Newton’s second law states that the acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the resultant force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass:

$$F = m a$$

Where \(F\) is the resultant force in newtons (N), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), and \(a\) is acceleration in m/s\(^2\).

This tells us three things: a larger force produces a greater acceleration; a larger mass requires a greater force for the same acceleration; and if the resultant force is zero, there is no acceleration.

A 1200 kg car has a driving force of 4800 N and friction of 1200 N. Calculate the acceleration.

Step 1: Resultant force = 4800 − 1200 = 3600 N

Step 2: \(a = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{3600}{1200} = 3\) m/s\(^2\)

Newton’s Third Law

Newton’s third law states that whenever two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other. These forces act on different objects and are always the same type of force.

Key Fact

Newton’s third law pairs always: act on two different objects, are the same size, act in opposite directions, and are the same type of force. For example, the Earth pulls you down with gravity, and you pull the Earth up with the same gravitational force.

Students often confuse balanced forces with Newton’s third law pairs. Balanced forces act on the same object (e.g. weight and normal force on a book). Newton’s third law pairs act on different objects (e.g. the book pushes the table down, the table pushes the book up).

Another misconception: “if the forces are equal and opposite, the object can’t move.” This is wrong because the two forces act on different objects. A rocket accelerates because the rocket pushes gas backwards and the gas pushes the rocket forwards — these act on different objects.

Terminal Velocity

When an object falls through a fluid (air or water), it initially accelerates due to gravity. As its speed increases, the drag force (air resistance) increases. Eventually, the drag force equals the weight and the resultant force becomes zero.

At this point, the object reaches terminal velocity — it continues to fall at a constant speed because the forces are balanced.

When a skydiver jumps, they accelerate because weight is greater than air resistance. As speed increases, air resistance increases, so acceleration decreases. At terminal velocity (~55 m/s), forces are balanced. When the parachute opens, air resistance suddenly increases above the weight, so the skydiver decelerates. A new, lower terminal velocity (~5 m/s) is reached.

physics-paper-2_L5.title: Stopping Distances, Braking and Momentum
physics-paper-2_L5.content_html:
What Are Stopping Distances?

When a vehicle needs to stop, it doesn't happen instantly. The stopping distance is made up of two parts: thinking distance and braking distance.

Key Fact

Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance

The thinking distance is how far the car travels while the driver reacts to a hazard. During this time, the vehicle continues at constant speed.

The braking distance is how far the car travels while the brakes are being applied and the vehicle is decelerating.

Several factors can increase thinking distance:

  • Tiredness or fatigue reduces reaction speed
  • Drugs and alcohol slow down the nervous system
  • Distractions like mobile phones delay reactions
  • Higher speeds mean more distance covered during reaction time

Braking Forces and Energy

When brakes are applied, friction between the brake pads and wheels creates a force that opposes motion. This braking force does work against the vehicle's kinetic energy.

The work done by braking forces transfers the vehicle's kinetic energy into heat energy at the brakes. We can calculate this using:

$$\text{Work done by brakes} = \text{Braking force} \times \text{Braking distance}$$

This work done equals the kinetic energy that was lost: \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2\)

Key Fact

Braking distance is proportional to the square of speed. Double the speed means four times the braking distance.

Braking distance increases when:

  • Vehicle speed is higher — kinetic energy increases with speed squared
  • Vehicle mass is greater — more kinetic energy to remove
  • Road conditions are poor — wet or icy roads reduce friction
  • Brake or tyre condition is poor — worn components reduce braking force

Understanding Momentum

Every moving object has momentum. Momentum is calculated using:

$$\text{momentum} = \text{mass} \times \text{velocity}$$

$$p = m \times v$$

Momentum is measured in kg⋅m/s and is a vector quantity — it has both size and direction.

In any collision or explosion, the total momentum before equals the total momentum after. This is the conservation of momentum.

For two objects colliding:

$$m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = m_1v_1 + m_2v_2$$

Where \(u\) represents initial velocities and \(v\) represents final velocities.

Vehicle Safety Features

Modern vehicles use momentum principles to improve safety during collisions. The key is to increase the time over which momentum changes occur.

Using \(F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}\), we can see that increasing the time (\(\Delta t\)) for a momentum change reduces the force experienced.

Key Fact

Safety features work by increasing collision time, which reduces the forces acting on passengers.

Examples of safety features include:

  • Crumple zones — designed to deform and extend collision time
  • Airbags — inflate to cushion impact and increase stopping time
  • Seat belts — stretch slightly to reduce peak forces on the body
  • ABS brakes — prevent wheel locking to maintain steering control

physics-paper-2_L8.title: Magnets, Electromagnetism and the Motor Effect
physics-paper-2_L8.content_html:
Permanent and Induced Magnets

A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field. It always has a north pole and a south pole. Like poles repel; unlike poles attract. Common permanent magnets are made from iron, steel, nickel, or cobalt.

An induced magnet is a material that becomes magnetic only when placed inside a magnetic field. When removed from the field, it quickly loses its magnetism. An induced magnet is always attracted to the permanent magnet, never repelled.

Key Fact

A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or magnetic material. Field lines go from north to south outside the magnet. The closer together the field lines, the stronger the field.

Place a compass near a bar magnet. Mark the position of the compass needle. Move the compass so the tail of the needle is at the mark you just made. Repeat to trace a complete field line. Alternatively, place the magnet under a sheet of paper and sprinkle iron filings on top — they align with the field lines.

Electromagnetism

When a current flows through a wire, it produces a magnetic field around the wire. The field lines form concentric circles around the wire. The direction of the field can be found using the right-hand rule: point your thumb in the direction of current, and your fingers curl in the direction of the field.

A solenoid is a coil of wire. When current flows through it, the magnetic field inside is strong and uniform (like a bar magnet). The strength of the field can be increased by: increasing the current, increasing the number of turns, or placing an iron core inside the solenoid.

Key Fact

An electromagnet is a solenoid with a soft iron core. It can be switched on and off by controlling the current. This makes electromagnets useful in scrapyard cranes, circuit breakers, electric bells, and MRI scanners.

The Motor Effect

When a current-carrying wire is placed in a magnetic field, it experiences a force. This is called the motor effect. The force is at its maximum when the wire is perpendicular to the magnetic field and zero when the wire is parallel to the field.

The size of the force is given by:

$$F = BIl$$

Where \(F\) is force in newtons, \(B\) is magnetic flux density in tesla (T), \(I\) is current in amps, and \(l\) is the length of wire in the field in metres.

Fleming’s left-hand rule predicts the direction of the force. Hold your left hand with the thumb, first finger, and second finger all at right angles. The first finger points in the direction of the magnetic field (north to south), the second finger points in the direction of conventional current, and the thumb shows the direction of the force (motion).

Electric Motors

A simple d.c. motor uses the motor effect to produce rotation. A coil of wire is placed between the poles of a magnet. When current flows, one side of the coil is pushed up and the other is pushed down (by the motor effect), creating a turning force.

A split-ring commutator reverses the direction of current in the coil every half turn. Without it, the coil would rotate 180° and then stop. The commutator ensures the forces always act in the right direction to keep the coil spinning continuously.

The speed of a motor can be increased by: increasing the current, using a stronger magnet, or adding more turns to the coil.
